dervis-irab:62-74.t:
* Vocabulary:
(نُزُلًا): al-nuzul, with two dammas or with a damma on the nūn and a sukūn on the zāy, is the lodging and whatever is prepared for the guest; the plural is anzāl. Al-nuzul, with two dammas, is also: blessed food; the lodging; the people who alight; the yield of what is sown and its growth; the gift and the bounty. It has been borrowed figuratively for the outcome of a thing: the outcome of the known provision is pleasure and joy, while the outcome of the zaqqūm tree is pain.
(الزَّقُّومِ): He said in al-Qāmūs: "al-zaqm is swallowing a morsel, and al-tazaqqum is gulping it down; azqamahu fa-izdaqamahu: he made him swallow and he swallowed. Al-zaqqūm, on the pattern of tannūr, is butter with dates, a tree in Hell, a plant in the desert with a flower shaped like jasmine, and the food of the people of the Fire." And he said in al-Asās: "You say: whoever denies that he will rise, Allah will feed him al-zaqqūm. It is said that the people of Ifrīqiya call butter with dates zaqqūm, and it comes from their saying:
that he gulps the morsels (yazqamu), and swallows them and gulps them down (yazdaqimuhā): he swallows them; and he spent the night gulping down (yatazaqqamu) milk if he drank it to excess." In al-Khāzin: al-zaqqūm is the fruit of a foul tree, bitter and repulsive in taste, which the people of the Fire are compelled to take, so they swallow it with the utmost loathing. It is also said that it is a tree found in the land of Tihāma, one of the foulest of trees. More will be said about the zaqqūm tree in the section on rhetoric.
(طَلْعُها): al-ṭalʿ in reality is the name of the fruit of the date palm at its first emergence, so applying it to the fruit of this tree is figurative, by way of metaphor, as will come in the section on rhetoric. The ṭalʿ of the palm is something that comes out as if it were two sandals folded together, with the fruit stacked between them, and it is whatever appears of its fruit at its first appearance.
(شوبا): with a fatḥa on the shīn, and it is a maṣdar (verbal noun) in its original sense. It is also said that the passive participle is meant by it, and the reading of some who read لشوبا with a damma indicates this. Al-Zajjāj said:
the form with fatḥa is a maṣdar and the form with damma is a noun meaning "the mixed", like al-naqḍ meaning "the broken down". The verb from it is shābahu yashūbuhu (of the pattern qāla) when he mixed it; and it is the mixture.
(حَمِيمٍ): hot water, which is what is intended here; it is also applied to cold water, so it is one of the words with opposite meanings (aḍdād).

* I'rab:
(أَذلِكَ خَيْرٌ نُزُلًا أَمْ شَجَرَةُ الزَّقُّومِ) The clause is the content of an omitted saying that goes back to the mention of the known provision; that is, "Say to them, Muhammad, by way of denial, rebuke and mockery: is that better as a lodging...". The hamza is for rebuking denial (istifhām inkārī) and rebuke; ذلك is the mubtadaʾ (subject), خير the khabar (predicate), and نزلا a tamyīz (specification) for خير; أم is a conjunction, and شجرة الزقوم is conjoined to ذلك. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The accusative of نزلا is as a tamyīz, and you may make it a ḥāl (circumstantial), as you say: is the palm tree better as unripe dates or as ripe dates?"
(إِنَّا جَعَلْناها فِتْنَةً لِلظَّالِمِينَ) inna and its noun; the clause جعلناها is the khabar; جعلناها is a verb, agent and first direct object; فتنة is the second direct object; and للظالمين is an adjective of فتنة, meaning a trial, a punishment and an affliction for them, because they said: the Fire burns trees, so how can it grow one?
(إِنَّها شَجَرَةٌ تَخْرُجُ فِي أَصْلِ الْجَحِيمِ) inna and its noun; شجرة is its khabar; the clause تخرج is an adjective of شجرة; and في أصل الجحيم is attached to تخرج.
(طَلْعُها كَأَنَّهُ رُؤُسُ الشَّياطِينِ) طلعها is the mubtadaʾ; the simile clause is the khabar; كأن and its noun, and رؤوس الشياطين is the khabar of كأن.
(فَإِنَّهُمْ لَآكِلُونَ مِنْها فَمالِؤُنَ مِنْهَا الْبُطُونَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; inna and its noun; the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); آكلون is the khabar of inna; منها is attached to آكلون; فمالئون: the fāʾ is a conjunction of sequence with immediacy; مالئون is conjoined to آكلون; منها is attached to مالئون; and البطون is the direct object of مالئون, because of the intensity of their hunger.
(ثُمَّ إِنَّ لَهُمْ عَلَيْها لَشَوْباً مِنْ حَمِيمٍ) ثم is a conjunction of sequence with delay; inna is a particle resembling the verb; لهم is its fronted khabar; عليها is attached to an omitted ḥāl; the shifted lām; شوبا is its delayed noun; and من حميم is an adjective of شوبا.
(ثُمَّ إِنَّ مَرْجِعَهُمْ لَإِلَى الْجَحِيمِ) ثم is a conjunction of sequence with delay; inna and its noun; the shifted lām; and إلى الجحيم is its khabar.
(إِنَّهُمْ أَلْفَوْا آباءَهُمْ ضالِّينَ) The clause gives the reason for the preceding, namely their being tried with kinds of punishment. inna and its noun; the clause ألفوا is its khabar; آباءهم is the first direct object of ألفوا and ضالين the second direct object of ألفوا.
(فَهُمْ عَلى آثارِهِمْ يُهْرَعُونَ) The fāʾ is causal; هم is the mubtadaʾ; على آثارهم is attached to يهرعون; and the clause يهرعون is the khabar of هم. Al-ihrāʿ is hurrying intensely, with urging and agitation. In al-Miṣbāḥ: harraʿa and uhriʿa, both with the passive form, when he is made to hurry.
(وَلَقَدْ ضَلَّ قَبْلَهُمْ أَكْثَرُ الْأَوَّلِينَ) The lām is the response to an omitted oath; قد is a particle of affirmation; ضل is a past verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa; قبلهم is an adverb attached to an omitted ḥāl; and أكثر الأولين is the agent.
(وَلَقَدْ أَرْسَلْنا فِيهِمْ مُنْذِرِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction; the lām is the response to an omitted oath; قد is a particle of affirmation; أرسلنا is a verb and agent; فيهم is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أرسلنا; and منذرين is the direct object.
(فَانْظُرْ كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ الْمُنْذَرِينَ) The fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ (al-fāʾ al-faṣīḥa); انظر is an imperative verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; كيف is an interrogative noun in the position of accusative, the fronted khabar of كان; عاقبة is its delayed noun; and المنذرين, with fatḥa on the dhāl, is the direct object (of the verbal noun, in the genitive construct).
(إِلَّا عِبادَ اللَّهِ الْمُخْلَصِينَ) إلا is a particle of exception meaning "but" (lākin), because the exception is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ); عباد الله is the excepted; and المخلصين is an adjective.

* Rhetoric:
These verses are rich in kinds of rhetoric. We shall expand on them and shall transmit to you full summaries of what the pillars of rhetoric have set down concerning them. The first of the arts in them is:
1- The simile with the heads of the devils:
This is the likening of the ṭalʿ of the zaqqūm tree to the heads of the devils, and it is an imaginary simile (tashbīh khayālī), already mentioned in what we presented earlier of the divisions of simile. We cite here the gist of what Ibn Rashīq said about it:
"Know that simile is of two kinds: a good simile and an ugly simile. The good simile is the one that brings out what is more obscure into what is clearer, so it yields clarity; the ugly simile is whatever is contrary to that." Al-Rummānī said: "The explanation of that is that what the sense perceives is clearer than what the sense does not perceive; the observed is clearer than the absent, so the first is clearer in the intellect than the second, and the third is clearer than the fourth; what a person perceives of himself is clearer than what he knows of others; the near is clearer than the far in general; and what is familiar is clearer than what is not familiar." Then Ibn Rashīq moved on to the simile found in the verse and said:
"Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: 'Its ṭalʿ is as if it were the heads of the devils.' Some said that the zaqqūm tree, which is also the ustun, has a repulsive form and an ugly fruit, called the heads of the devils." And the ustun, as al-Majd says:
"al-ustun and al-ustān, with a fatḥa on the hamza and a sukūn on the sīn in both, are the roots of trees that spread over their growing places, so that when the beholder looks at them he likens them to the figures of people." Until he says: "The best and most known is that it was likened to what no one doubts is repulsive and ugly, because of what Allah the Mighty and Majestic placed in the hearts of mankind of the horror of the forms of the jinn."
A splendid passage by al-Jāḥiẓ:
How we wished that the book "Naẓm al-Qur'an" were available to us, so that we might read the splendid passage that al-Jāḥiẓ wrote on this simile. But the book is lost, with what was lost of our Arabic legacy, so we must transmit fragments from it that occur in his other books. In Kitāb al-Ḥayawān is the following text: "It is not that people ever saw a devil in any form; but since Allah the Exalted placed in the nature of all nations the finding ugly of all forms of devils, and the loathing and dislike of them, and made proverbs about that run on the tongues of all of them, the matter returned, by way of frightening, repelling, alarming and rebuking, to what Allah had placed in the natures of the earlier and later peoples and among all nations, contrary to the natures of all nations. This interpretation is more fitting than the saying of those exegetes who claimed that the heads of the devils are a plant that grows in Yemen."
Al-Jāḥiẓ addressed this simile once more and said: "Some people claimed that the heads of the devils are the fruit of a tree found in the land of Yemen with a loathsome appearance. But the theologians do not know this interpretation and said: only the heads of the devils known by this name were meant, from the wicked and rebellious among the jinn. Then the people of criticism and dissent said: it is not permissible to coin a proverb with something we have not seen so that we could picture it, nor whose form has been described to us in a speaking book or a truthful report. The way the speech comes out indicates that the intimidation is with that form and the terrifying by it, and that had there been anything more effective in deterrence than that, it would have mentioned it. How could that be so, when people are frightened only by something dreadful and hideous that they have seen, or that a truthful, eloquent describer has pictured for them, whereas we have never encountered them and no truthful person has pictured them for us? Moreover, most people of those nations that have not lived alongside the People of the two Books and the bearers of the Qur'an among the Muslims, and have not heard the disagreement, do not imagine that, do not stop at it and are not frightened by it, so how can it be a general threat? We said: even if we have never seen a devil, and no truthful person has drawn its heads for us with his hand, in their unanimity on coining a proverb with the ugliness of the devil, such that they use it in two ways, one of which is to say, 'he is uglier than the devil', and the other is that the beautiful is called a devil by way of averting the evil eye, just as a noble mare is called shawhāʾ (ugly), and a beautiful woman is called ṣammāʾ (deaf), qarnāʾ (horned), khansāʾ (snub-nosed), jarbāʾ (mangy) and the like, by way of averting the evil eye; in the unanimity of the Muslims, the Arabs and everyone we have met on coining a proverb with the ugliness of the devil, there is evidence that in reality he is uglier than every ugly thing."
In this passage al-Jāḥiẓ detailed the aspects of the simile and the Qur'anic style's handling of the thing likened to and the point of resemblance, which it derives without sensory perception, relying on its being established in perception by custom, convention and people's passing it on. Al-Jāḥiẓ allowed such a simile, explained its purport, and discussed the views of others on the necessity of relying on visual sense to depict the meaning in the mind. From that time, or a little earlier, people took an interest in these two kinds of simile and followed them in the Qur'an and in eloquence generally; the studies of rhetoric revolved around this point, and other kinds branched off from these two. Thus this verse, and its like, had an effect in drawing people's attention to simile. Abū ʿUbayda studied it in them, and al-Jāḥiẓ renewed the study and expanded on it, and the verse remained at the head of the examples of conceptual simile in the books of criticism and rhetoric after the two of them.
Al-Jāḥiẓ rejected the sensory interpretation of the linguists, which agrees with the view of the literalists in exegesis and also opposes the view of the people of speculation among the theologians and the Muʿtazila. Those had interpreted the heads of the devils as the heads of a plant growing in Yemen, or a tree of loathsome appearance, or snakes of ugly shape; all of which are material referents of the word "devil" that may have some basis in reality or may be their own invention. In either case their effect on the soul does not reach that of the image of the devil that leaps to the imagination and gathers every trait of terror and ugliness, even if it is not as clear as the plant, the tree and the snakes; and this vagueness lends it additional intimidation.
Therefore al-Jāḥiẓ's interpretation was more perceptive of the aim of the Qur'anic expression in the souls, a perception of value from the critical standpoint, namely the effect of literature on the soul. These are passing remarks in the books of the ancients, which modern criticism has taken care of. He mentions examples of simile with animals in the Qur'an, because of the predominance of a certain attribute in each kind that the context wished to highlight: Allah coins a proverb with the spider for the frailty and weakness of its house, with the donkey for ignorance, heedlessness, scant knowledge and coarseness of nature, and with the ape for ugliness, deformity and baseness of soul.
Perhaps this verse, or rather this simile, is what led Abū ʿUbayda to compose his book "Majāz al-Qur'an", which we have not seen, but which is mentioned by Ibn al-Nadīm, author of al-Fihrist, al-Khaṭīb, author of Tārīkh Baghdād, Ibn al-Anbārī in Nuzhat al-Alibbāʾ, Yāqūt in Irshād al-Arīb, Ibn Khallikān in al-Wafayāt, and al-Suyūṭī in Bughyat al-Wuʿāh. Yāqūt mentions that Abū ʿUbayda wrote the book al-Majāz in the year 188 of the Prophet's hijra, ﷺ, reporting on the authority of Abū ʿUbayda:
"Al-Faḍl ibn al-Rabīʿ sent for me to come to him in the year 188, so I came to Baghdad and asked permission to see him, and he granted it. He was in a long, wide assembly hall containing a single carpet that filled it, and at its head were high cushions that could be reached only by a stool. Then a man in the dress of the secretaries, of imposing bearing, entered, and he seated him beside me and said to him: do you know this man? He said: no. He said: this is Abū ʿUbayda, the great scholar of the people of Basra; we brought him so that we may benefit from his knowledge. The man prayed for him and praised him for this deed, and said: I have longed for you, and I have a question; will you permit me to put it to you? I said:
go ahead. He said: Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: 'Its ṭalʿ is as if it were the heads of the devils.' Promise and threat are made only with what its like is known, and this is not known. I said: Allah the Exalted addressed the Arabs only according to their own manner of speech. Have you not heard the words of Imruʾ al-Qays:
أيقتلني والمشرفي مضاجعي ... ومسنونة زرق كأنياب أغوال
(Will he kill me, when the Mashrafī sword is my bedfellow, and sharpened blue-grey arrowheads like the fangs of ghouls?)
They had never seen the ghoul, but since the matter of the ghoul terrified them, they threatened with it. Al-Faḍl approved of that, and the questioner approved of it, and on that day I resolved to compose a book on the Qur'an about such things and their like, and what is needed of its knowledge. When I returned to Basra I composed my book which I called 'al-Majāz'."
The wording of al-Samīn on this point: "His saying 'as if it were the heads of the devils' has two aspects. The first is that it is literal, and that the head of the devils is a particular tree in a region called al-Ustun, a bitter tree of repulsive form which the Arabs so named by likening it to the heads of the devils in ugliness, and then it became a base to which things are likened. It is also said that the devils are a kind of snake; and it is said to be a tree called al-ṣirm. On this view the Arabs were addressed with what they know, and this tree exists, so the speech is literal. The second is that it belongs to the category of representation and imagination (tamthīl and takhayyul), because everything that is found repulsive and ugly in nature and form is likened to what imagination pictures even if it has not been seen; and the devils, though existent, are not seen by the Arabs, but He addressed them with the figures of speech they were familiar with."
As for al-Zamakhsharī, he gathered all the views together but put first the one that is preferable, saying in his delightful style: "The ṭalʿ belongs to the palm, and was borrowed for what comes out of the zaqqūm tree of its fruit, whether as a verbal or a conceptual metaphor, and it was likened to the heads of the devils as an indication of its utmost repulsiveness and ugliness of appearance, because the devil is hateful and found ugly in the natures of people, since they believe he is pure evil with no good mixed in. So they say of one ugly in form, 'as if he had the face of a devil', 'as if he had the head of a devil'; and when painters depict him they bring his image in the ugliest form whose dread they can manage, just as they believed of the angel that he is pure good with no evil in him, so they liken a beautiful form to him. Allah the Exalted said: 'This is not a human being; this is but a noble angel.' This is an imaginary simile. It is also said that the devil is a crested snake (ḥayya ʿurfāʾ) with a very ugly, dreadful appearance; and it is said that there is a tree called al-ustun, rough, bitter, stinking and of repulsive form, whose fruit is called the heads of the devils. The Arabs called this fruit the heads of the devils only with the intention of one of the two similes, but after being so named it returned as a third base to which things are likened."
2- The secret of the conjunction with "thumma":
In His saying "Then indeed they will have upon it a mixture of boiling water" there is a secret subtle in its derivation and precise in its path, to which few attend. For the meaning of delay has two aspects:
One: that they fill their bellies from the zaqqūm tree, which is hot and burns their bellies and increases their thirst and parching, so they are given nothing to drink until after a long while, as torment by that thirst; then they are given to drink what is hotter than the thirst, namely the drink mixed with boiling water. The second aspect is that He mentioned the food with that repulsiveness and hideousness, and then mentioned the drink with what is yet deeper in repulsiveness and further in hideousness; so He brought "thumma" to indicate the distance of the state of the drink from the state of the food and the difference of its description from its description in exceeding it. The meaning of the second is that they are taken from their dwellings and abodes in Hell, which are the levels in which they are lodged, to the zaqqūm tree, and they eat until they fill their bellies, and are given to drink after that, and then return to their levels. The meaning of delay in that is clear and understandable.

dervis-irab:133-138.t:
* I'rab:
(وَإِنَّ لُوطاً لَمِنَ الْمُرْسَلِينَ) This is the fifth story. The wāw is resumptive (istiʾnāfiyya) or conjunctive; inna and its noun; the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); and «مِنَ الْمُرْسَلِينَ» is its predicate.
(إِذْ نَجَّيْناهُ وَأَهْلَهُ أَجْمَعِينَ) The adverbial «إِذْ» is attached to an omitted verb, its implied form being "Remember" (udhkur). The clause «نَجَّيْناهُ», consisting of verb, agent and object, is in the position of the genitive, because the adverbial is annexed to it. «وَأَهْلَهُ» is a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment) or is conjoined to the hāʾ; «أَجْمَعِينَ» is tawkīd (emphasis).
(إِلَّا عَجُوزاً فِي الْغابِرِينَ) «إِلَّا» is a particle of exception, «عَجُوزاً» is the excepted, and «فِي الْغابِرِينَ» is an adjective. (ثُمَّ دَمَّرْنَا الْآخَرِينَ)
«ثُمَّ» is a conjunction of sequence with delay; «دَمَّرْنَا الْآخَرِينَ» is a past verb, an agent and a direct object; they are the disbelievers of his people.
(وَإِنَّكُمْ لَتَمُرُّونَ عَلَيْهِمْ مُصْبِحِينَ)
The wāw is conjunctive or circumstantial (ḥāliyya); inna and its noun; the shifted lām; «تَمُرُّونَ» is an imperfect verb and an agent; «عَلَيْهِمْ» is attached to «تَمُرُّونَ»; «مُصْبِحِينَ» is a ḥāl (circumstantial), and it is a complete one. (وَبِاللَّيْلِ أَفَلا تَعْقِلُونَ)
The wāw is conjunctive; «وَبِاللَّيْلِ» is conjoined to «مُصْبِحِينَ», so it is another ḥāl; the ḥāl here is construed as referring to place, and the bāʾ expresses accompaniment (mulābasa). The hamza enters upon an implied clause on which His words «فَلا تَعْقِلُونَ» are conjoined, the implied form being: "You witness that, and so do you not understand?", that is, "do you not take a lesson from it?"

dervis-irab:139-156.t:
* Vocabulary:
(أَبَقَ)
: He fled from his people without the permission of his Lord. The verb properly applies only to a slave, who flees from his master, but it was applied to Yūnus (Jonah) by way of explicit metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya) of the derivative kind, or by way of metonymy (majāz mursal) whose relation is the use of the restricted for the unrestricted. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "«أبق العبد أبقا» (the slave ran away), from the bābs of taʿiba and qatala in one dialect, though most often from the bāb of ḍaraba, when he flees from his master without fear and without hardship. «الإباق» with kasra is the noun from it; he is an «آبق» (runaway), and the plural is «أبّاق», like «كافر» and «كفار»."
(الْمُدْحَضِينَ)
: Those overcome by the casting of lots. «ساهم» means that he cast lots with the people of the ship and was overcome by the lot. The story of Yūnus will be given in brief in the section on Benefits.
(مُلِيمٌ) : One who has entered into blame. It is said «ألام فلان» when someone did what deserves blame. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "«لامه لوما» (from the bāb of qāla): he reproached him, so he is «ملوم» (blamed) in respect of the shortcoming, and the agent is «لائم»; the plural is «لوم», like «راكع» and «ركع». «ألامه» with an alif is a dialectal form, so he is «ملام» and the agent is «مليم»; the noun is «الملامة», and the plural is «ملاوم»; «اللائمة» is like «الملامة». «ألام الرجل» when he did something for which he deserves blame; «تلوّم تلوما» means to linger."
(العراء) : An empty place with no tree and nothing covering it. It is derived from «العري», which is the absence of covering; the barren earth was likened to that because nothing covers it. «العرا» with a short vowel is the side, and from it comes «اعتراه», meaning he made for its side. The wording of al-Qāmūs: "«العراء» is open space in which one is not hidden by anything; its plural is «إعراء»; and «أعرى» means he travelled in it and stayed."
(يَقْطِينٍ) : Al-Qāmūs says: "A plant and the like that has no stem; and, with the feminine ending, the fresh gourd." The wording of al-Zamakhsharī: "«اليقطين» is everything that lies stretched out on the face of the earth and does not stand on a stem, like the plant of the watermelon, the cucumber and the colocynth. It is of the form «يفعيل» from «قطن بالمكان» when he stayed in it. It is also said that it is the gourd (al-dubbāʾ)." The gourd was singled out only because it combines the coolness of shade, a soft touch and large leaves, and because flies do not approach it.

* I'rab:
(وَإِنَّ يُونُسَ لَمِنَ الْمُرْسَلِينَ)
Resumptive or conjunctive, introduced to relate the sixth story, the story of Yūnus, peace be upon him; a full summary of it will come in the section on Benefits. Inna and its noun, the shifted lām, and «مِنَ الْمُرْسَلِينَ» is the predicate of inna. (إِذْ أَبَقَ إِلَى الْفُلْكِ الْمَشْحُونِ)
«إِذْ» is an adverbial attached to «الْمُرْسَلِينَ», meaning "he was of the messengers even in this state"; the clause «أَبَقَ» is in the position of the genitive, since the adverbial is annexed to it; «إِلَى الْفُلْكِ» is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to «أَبَقَ», and «الْمَشْحُونِ» is an adjective.
(فَساهَمَ فَكانَ مِنَ الْمُدْحَضِينَ)
The fāʾ is conjunctive; «ساهَمَ» is a past verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he"; «فَكانَ» is conjoined to «فَساهَمَ», and its noun is latent, its implied form being "he"; «مِنَ الْمُدْحَضِينَ» is the predicate of kāna. (فَالْتَقَمَهُ الْحُوتُ وَهُوَ مُلِيمٌ) The fāʾ is conjoined to an omitted clause understood from the context, namely "so they threw him into the sea, and the whale swallowed him"; it is also said, "so he threw himself into the water." «الْتَقَمَهُ» is a verb with a fronted direct object, and «الْحُوتُ» is a postponed mubtadaʾ; the wāw is circumstantial; «هُوَ» is a mubtadaʾ and «مُلِيمٌ» a khabar, and the clause is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl. The meaning is that he had done something for which he deserved blame.
(فَلَوْلا أَنَّهُ كانَ مِنَ الْمُسَبِّحِينَ) The fāʾ is conjunctive; «لَوْلا» is a particle expressing prevention of one thing due to the existence of another; «أَنَّ» and what follows it form a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is necessarily omitted; anna and its noun, and the clause «كانَ» is its predicate; the noun of kāna is latent, its implied form being "he", and «مِنَ الْمُسَبِّحِينَ» is its predicate.
(لَلَبِثَ فِي بَطْنِهِ إِلى يَوْمِ يُبْعَثُونَ) The lām occurs in the apodosis of «لولا»; «لَبِثَ» is a past verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he"; «فِي بَطْنِهِ» is attached to «لَبِثَ» or to an omitted ḥāl, that is, "remaining"; «إِلى يَوْمِ» is attached to «لَبِثَ»; the clause «يُبْعَثُونَ» is that to which the adverbial is annexed; «يُبْعَثُونَ» is a passive imperfect verb, and the wāw is the nāʾib fāʿil. (فَنَبَذْناهُ بِالْعَراءِ وَهُوَ سَقِيمٌ) The fāʾ is conjoined to an omitted clause, namely "We commanded the whale to cast him out, so We cast him out"; «نَبَذْناهُ» is a verb, an agent and a direct object; «بِالْعَراءِ» is attached to «نَبَذْناهُ»; the wāw is circumstantial; «هُوَ» is a mubtadaʾ and «سَقِيمٌ» a khabar, that is, ailing from what had befallen him. (وَأَنْبَتْنا عَلَيْهِ شَجَرَةً مِنْ يَقْطِينٍ) «أَنْبَتْنا» is conjoined to «فَنَبَذْناهُ»; «عَلَيْهِ» is attached to «أَنْبَتْنا»; «شَجَرَةً» is a direct object, and «مِنْ يَقْطِينٍ» is an adjective of «شَجَرَةً». (وَأَرْسَلْناهُ إِلى مِائَةِ أَلْفٍ أَوْ يَزِيدُونَ) The wāw is a conjunction; «أَرْسَلْنا» is a verb, an agent and a direct object; «إِلى مِائَةِ أَلْفٍ» is attached to «أَرْسَلْناهُ»; «أَوْ» is a conjunction; «يَزِيدُونَ» is an imperfect verb in the nominative. A detailed discussion of «أو» will come in the section on Benefits. (فَآمَنُوا فَمَتَّعْناهُمْ إِلى حِينٍ) The fāʾ is conjunctive; «آمَنُوا» is a past verb indeclinable on the ḍamma, and the wāw is the agent; the fāʾ is conjunctive; «مَتَّعْناهُمْ» is a verb, an agent and a direct object; «إِلى حِينٍ» is attached to «مَتَّعْناهُمْ».
(فَاسْتَفْتِهِمْ أَلِرَبِّكَ الْبَناتُ وَلَهُمُ الْبَنُونَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; this clause is conjoined to His words «فَاسْتَفْتِهِمْ» even though the distance is great. Al-Bayḍāwī said:
"«فاستفتهم» is conjoined to its like at the beginning of the sura. He first commanded that they be questioned about the denial of the Resurrection, and the discourse moved on, in that connection, to stories suited to it, joined one to another. Then He commanded that they be questioned about the division, since they made daughters for Allah and sons for themselves in their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah." It has already been said that the first fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa (the eloquent fāʾ), because it occurs in the apodosis of an implied condition. A debate has arisen about this distant conjunction, which we will treat in detail in the section on Benefits. «اسْتَفْتِهِمْ» is an imperative verb, its agent a latent pronoun whose implied form is "you", and the hāʾ is a direct object; the hamza is for rebuking interrogation (istifhām inkārī), whose meaning will come in the section on Rhetoric; «لِرَبِّكَ» is a fronted khabar and «الْبَناتُ» a postponed mubtadaʾ; the wāw is a conjunction; «لَهُمُ» is a fronted khabar and «الْبَنُونَ» a postponed mubtadaʾ. (أَمْ خَلَقْنَا الْمَلائِكَةَ إِناثاً وَهُمْ شاهِدُونَ) «أَمْ» is a conjunction corresponding to the hamza (muʿādila), as though the questioner claims that one of two things is established and asks them to specify it, saying: "Which of these two things do you claim?" «خَلَقْنَا» is a verb and an agent; «الْمَلائِكَةَ» is a direct object; «إِناثاً» is a ḥāl; the wāw is circumstantial; «هُمْ» is a mubtadaʾ and «شاهِدُونَ» a khabar, and the clause is in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl.
(أَلا إِنَّهُمْ مِنْ إِفْكِهِمْ لَيَقُولُونَ) A resumptive statement introduced to refute their corrupt doctrine by showing that it is a plain falsehood supported by no evidence. «أَلا» is a particle of alerting; inna and its noun; «مِنْ إِفْكِهِمْ» is attached to «يَقُولُونَ»; the shifted lām; and the clause «يَقُولُونَ» is the khabar of «إِنَّهُمْ». (وَلَدَ اللَّهُ وَإِنَّهُمْ لَكاذِبُونَ) «وَلَدَ اللَّهُ» is a verb and an agent, and the clause is the content of their saying; the wāw is circumstantial; inna and its noun, the shifted lām, and «كاذِبُونَ» is its predicate. (أَصْطَفَى الْبَناتِ عَلَى الْبَنِينَ) The open hamza is for rebuking interrogation; it dispenses with the hamzat al-waṣl, which is used to reach a sukūn-initial letter in pronunciation. «اصْطَفَى» is a past verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "He", referring to Allah; «الْبَناتِ» is a direct object; «عَلَى الْبَنِينَ» is attached to «اصْطَفَى» after it has been given the sense of "preferred". (ما لَكُمْ كَيْفَ تَحْكُمُونَ) «ما» is an interrogative noun; «لَكُمْ» is the khabar, meaning "what is established and fixed for you?", by way of rebuke; the clause is resumptive. «كَيْفَ» is an interrogative noun in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl or as a mafʿūl muṭlaq; «تَحْكُمُونَ» is an imperfect verb and an agent, and the clause is also resumptive, so neither of the two clauses is connected to the other.
(أَفَلا تَذَكَّرُونَ) The hamza is also for rebuking interrogation; the fāʾ is conjoined to an omitted clause understood from the context, namely "Have you gone blind to the truths and strayed from the evidences?"; «لا» is a negative particle; «تَذَكَّرُونَ» is an imperfect verb in the nominative and an agent, originally «تتذكرون»; the object of «تَذَكَّرُونَ» is omitted, its implied form being "that He is exalted above having a child".
(أَمْ لَكُمْ سُلْطانٌ مُبِينٌ) «أَمْ» is a conjunction meaning «بل», so it is for a transitional break-off (iḍrāb intiqālī); «لَكُمْ» is a fronted khabar, «سُلْطانٌ» a postponed mubtadaʾ, and «مُبِينٌ» an adjective of «سُلْطانٌ».

* Rhetoric:
In these verses the Meccan style is clear in its indication, plain in its sense and keen in feeling. The rebuking interrogation is repeated in them, censuring their ignorance, excessive in its dullness, which rests on three ignorances. The first is anthropomorphism, because begetting is among the properties of bodies. The second is preferring themselves over their Lord, since they made for Him the lowlier of the two sexes in their convention and understanding, and the loftier for themselves; that is an ignorance beyond which there is none. The third is that they belittled the most honoured of Allah's creatures and the nearest to Him, in that they made them female, although they used to reproach one another with the attribute of femininity and regard it as a sign of abasement and a mark of baseness.

* Benefits:
1- There is much disagreement about this «أو». Al-Farrāʾ said that its meaning is «بل يزيدون» ("rather they exceed"), so for him it is for iḍrāb (break-off). The first statement is according to what appears to people when they see them, and the second is a break-off from that in favour of what is actually the case in reality. The meaning is: "We sent him to a company that people would estimate at a hundred thousand, while they were more than that." There is a fine point in this, namely moving from the lower to the higher because of its impact on the soul and its drawing of attention, as opposed to reporting the higher from the start. Some of the Kufans said it has the meaning of «و» (and). As for the Basrans, they have several views on it:
1- It was said that it is for vagueness (ibhām).
2- It was said that it is for choice (takhyīr), that is, when an observer sees them he may choose between saying "they are a hundred thousand" or "they are more". Ibn Hishām said: Ibn al-Shajarī transmitted this view from Sībawayh, but its being established from him is open to question, and choice between two things, one of which has actually occurred, is not valid.
3- It was said that it is for doubt, attributed to the observer.
4- It was said that it is for permission (ibāḥa), that is, you may estimate them and reckon their number as you wish.
5- It was said that it is for doubt, in the sense that the most accurate of estimators would be in doubt about their number.
The best of what we have read is the statement of al-Zamakhsharī: "In the sight of the beholder", that is, when the beholder sees them he says: "They are a hundred thousand or more", the purpose being to describe them as numerous.
2- The distant conjunction:
His words «فاستفتهم» (the verse) are conjoined to what precedes, namely His words «فاستفتهم أهم أشد خلقا». The grammarians have forbidden separation by a clause, so what of separation by many clauses, indeed by a whole sura? But what the grammarians found objectionable applies to the conjunction of single words; as for clauses, because of their independence it is overlooked in them. And this discourse, because of its cohesion and interlocking, has become as one clause, so the distance is removed from it.
3- A summary of the story of Yūnus:
Dhū al-Nūn became angry with his people when the punishment he had promised them did not descend upon their courtyard, and so he went away in anger. It was not right for him to go; he was narrow in patience and short in endurance. When he boarded the ship, it stopped in the depths of the sea, and its sailors said: "Here is a slave who has run away from his master, whom the lot will reveal." It was their custom that if a ship carried a runaway or a sinner it did not sail. That was on the Tigris, for he had been sent to the people of Nineveh in the land of Mosul. When he cast lots, that is, when the people of the ship cast lots, he was among those overcome by the lot, so they threw him into the sea and the whale swallowed him, and so on to the end of that wonderful story.

dervis-irab:75-82.t:
* I'rab:
(وَلَقَدْ نادانا نُوحٌ فَلَنِعْمَ الْمُجِيبُونَ) A resumptive passage (kalām mustaʾnaf) introduced to begin detailing what was summarised earlier. The lām is the response to an omitted oath; قد is a particle of affirmation; نادانا نوح is a verb, a fronted direct object and a delayed agent. The fāʾ is a conjunction, and the lām is the response to an omitted oath; the response of each of the two oaths is omitted, as the context indicates it, and the implied form is: "By Allah, Noah called upon Us when he despaired of the belief of his people after having spent a thousand years less fifty among them, and they increased only in insolence, arrogance and aversion, so We answered him in the best manner of answering; and by Allah, how excellent are the Answerers, We." نعم is a rigid past verb for expressing praise; المجيبون is the agent of نعم; and the one specified for praise is omitted, its implied form being "We". This is the first of six stories that will follow in sequence.
(وَنَجَّيْناهُ وَأَهْلَهُ مِنَ الْكَرْبِ الْعَظِيمِ) The wāw is a conjunction; نجيناه is a verb, agent and direct object; أهله is conjoined to the hāʾ, or is a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment); من الكرب is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to نجيناه; and العظيم is an adjective of الكرب.
(وَجَعَلْنا ذُرِّيَّتَهُ هُمُ الْباقِينَ) وجعلنا is conjoined to نجيناه; ذريته is the direct object; هم is a separation pronoun (ḍamīr faṣl) with no position; and الباقين is the second direct object of جعلنا.
(وَتَرَكْنا عَلَيْهِ فِي الْآخِرِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction; تركنا is a verb and agent; عليه is an adjective of the omitted direct object, i.e. "praise being upon him"; and في الآخرين is in the position of accusative, a second direct object of تركنا. Something other than this has been said in the parsing of this verse.
(سَلامٌ عَلى نُوحٍ فِي الْعالَمِينَ) سلام is a mubtadaʾ, and what permits beginning with it (an indefinite) is the meaning of supplication it contains; على نوح is the khabar, attached to an omitted adjective of سلام, or attached to what the first is attached to. The clause سلام على نوح في العالمين is explicative of تركنا. Al-Samīn said: "His saying سلام على نوح is a mubtadaʾ and khabar, and there are several aspects to it. One is that it explains تركنا, i.e. We left upon him something, and it is this saying. It is also said that there is an implied saying, i.e. 'and We said: peace'. It is also said that تركنا was made to include the meaning of 'We said'. It is also said that تركنا was given governance over what follows. Al-Zamakhsharī said:
'and We left upon him among the later generations' this word, which is سلام على نوح في العالمين, meaning they greet him with a greeting and pray for him; and it is of the category of quoted speech, as in your saying 'a sūra which We have sent down'. What he said is the view of the Kufans, who made the clause in the position of accusative as the direct object of تركنا, not because it includes the meaning of saying, but it is on its own meaning, unlike the preceding aspect; and this too is among their views.'"
(إِنَّا كَذلِكَ نَجْزِي الْمُحْسِنِينَ) inna and its noun; كذلك is an adjective of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun); the clause نجزي is the khabar of inna; the agent of نجزي is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "We"; and المحسنين is the direct object of نجزي. The clause gives the reason for the recompense of Noah with that lofty honour, namely the eternity of his mention and the greeting of the worlds upon him for all time.
(إِنَّهُ مِنْ عِبادِنَا الْمُؤْمِنِينَ) A reason for the doing of good by faith, extolling the standing of faith, honouring it and urging an increase of it. inna and its noun; من عبادنا is its khabar; and المؤمنين is an adjective of عبادنا.
(ثُمَّ أَغْرَقْنَا الْآخَرِينَ) Conjoined to نجيناه وأهله. The sequence is real, because their deliverance took place before the drowning of the rest, but there is a delay between the two.

dervis-irab:1-10.t:
* Vocabulary:
(دُحُوراً): the verbal noun of دحره, meaning "he drove him away and removed him far"; it belongs to the pattern of خضع.
When the letter dāl is joined with ḥāʾ as the first and second radicals of the verb, the sense is one of throwing, driving away and pushing. Examples: دح الشيء في الأرض, i.e. he thrust it into the ground; دح الطعام بطنه, the food filled his belly until it hung down; دح الرجل, he shoved him on the nape of his neck, a usage the common people employ, saying "he shoved him (دحّه) on his back", so it is a case of eloquent colloquial speech. دحرج الشيء فتدحرج means he overturned the thing and made it revolve upon itself continuously down a slope, so that it rolled over.
دحس بين القوم means he stirred up mischief among the people; دحس الشيء means he filled it; دحس برجله means he scraped with his foot. One says "I have nothing of dāḥis", which is a swelling (disarray) of the finger and the falling off of the nail — what the common people call a hot swelling at the tip of the finger — and it is genuine eloquent Arabic. Muzarrid said:
تشاخت إبهاماك إن كنت كاذبا ... ولا برئا من داحس وكناع
(May your two thumbs gush blood if you are lying, and may they not be cured of dāḥis and kunāʿ.)
Al-Ḥajjāj went out one night and heard a dreadful voice, and said: "If this is someone with ʿāʾir or qādiḥ or dāḥis, do nothing; otherwise pull his tongue out from the back of his neck" — that is, someone with an eye ailment or a toothache. One says of a man or a beast that, when wounded, kicks in the throes of death: "I left him struggling (يفحص) and scraping (يدحص) the ground with his foot." دحضت رجله means his foot slipped, a slipping (daḥḍan and duḥūḍan); أدحض فلان قدمه means so-and-so made his foot slip; مزلقة مدحاض and "this is a slippery place for the foot" (مدحضة القدم); and دحض الحجة means he invalidated the argument.
دحقه يدحقه, from the pattern of فتح, daḥqan: he drove him away and removed him far. دحقت الرحم بساء الفحل means the womb cast out the stallion's seed and did not accept it; دحقت الحامل بولدها means the pregnant female miscarried her young; a "daḥīq" is a miscarried young one. It is also said: دحقت به means she gave birth to it. She is afflicted with دحاق, which is when her womb comes out after birth; she is then called دحوق or داحق. أدحقه الله means Allah put him far from good, and he is "daḥīq"; you say: "May Allah make him distant (أسحقه) and drive him away (أدحقه)", and he is "saḥīq daḥīq". دحل means he hid in a دحل, which is a hidden pit, narrow at the top and wide at the bottom; you say: "They sought blood-vengeance (الذحول) and hid in the pits (الدحول)." دحل البئر means he dug into the sides of a well; and the hunter set up الدواحيل, which are traps for wild asses, the singular being داحول; and "a well that is دحول" is one having تلحف, which is the breaking away of its sides because the water has eaten them. What the common people use of this is distorted and does not occur in the language in this sense except by a remote figurative extension; and their naming, lastly, of the "المدحلة" (steamroller) in its common sense is a laxity, but we too are lax about it.
دحمه دحما means he pushed him violently; so the common people's use of it in this sense is unobjectionable. دحمس الليل means the night grew dark or cast its darkness over everything. دحمل به means he rolled him on the ground. دحا الله الأرض means Allah spread it out and extended it; and دحا المطر الحصى عن وجه الأرض means the rain pushed the pebbles off the face of the earth; its pattern is that of نصر and فتح; one says دحا يدحو and دحى يدحى. The meaning of "spreading" does not imply that it is not like a ball; rather it is extended and broad, just as the baker takes the dough ball (الفرزدقة) and flattens it (يدحوها). Ibn al-Rūmī said:
ما أنسى لا أنسى خبازا مررت به ... يدحو الرّقاقة مثل اللمح بالبصر
ما بين رؤيتها في كفه كرة ... وبين رؤيتها قوراء كالقمر
إلا بمقدار ما تنداح دائرة ... في لجة الماء يرمي فيه بالحجر
(I shall not forget — I shall not forget — a baker I passed, who flattens the thin loaf as quick as a glance of the eye. Between seeing it a ball in his palm and seeing it a wide round like the moon is only the time a circle takes to spread out in the deep water into which a stone is thrown.)
This is among the wonders of our noble Arabic language.
(واصِبٌ): permanent. In al-Mukhtār: وصب الشيء يصب, with kasra, wuṣūban, means it was permanent; from it comes the saying of the Exalted «وله الدين واصبا» and His saying «ولهم عذاب واصب».
(فَأَتْبَعَهُ): In al-Mukhtār: تبعه, from the pattern of طرب, if he walked behind him or passed by him and went along with him; likewise اتبعه, which is on the pattern of افتعل, while أتبعه is on the pattern of أفعل. Al-Akhfash said: تبعه and أتبعه have the same meaning, like ردفه and أردفه; and from it is the saying of the Exalted «فأتبعه شهاب ثاقب».
(ثاقِبٌ): that is, it pierces it or burns it. Al-Qurṭubī reported two views in the exegesis of "ثاقب": one, that it means "shining", and the other that it means "kindled", from the saying اثقب زندك, "kindle your fire-stick", i.e. kindle your fire. Al-Bayḍāwī said: "ثاقب means shining, as if it pierces the air with its light." This root has marvels of variety and inflection. In al-Asās and al-Lisān: ثقب الشيء بالمثقب, he pierced the thing with the awl; ثقب القداح عينه, the cupping vessel pierced its spring so that the settled water came out; ثقب اللآل الدر, the pearl-merchant pierced the pearls, and a pearl is "mutaqqab"; and "he has virgin pearls", i.e. unpierced ones; and women pierced the face-veils for their eyes. Al-Muthaqqib al-ʿAbdī said:
أرين محاسنا وكننّ أخرى ... وثقبن الوصاوص للعيون
(They showed some charms and hid others, and they pierced the face-veil slits for the eyes.)
From this he was named al-Muthaqqib. A كوكب ثاقب and درّيء is a star intensely bright and sparkling, as if it pierces the darkness and penetrates it and drives it off. A man or woman "thaqīb" is likened to a flame of fire in the intensity of their redness, and there is in them "thaqāba". حسب ثاقب means famed lineage; رجل ثاقب الرأي is a man of sound, penetrating judgement who looks keenly. "A piercing eye came to me from you" means certain news. ثقب الطائر means the bird soared as if piercing the sky; and ثقّب الشيب في اللحية means grey hair began to appear in the sides of the beard.

* I'rab:
(وَالصَّافَّاتِ صَفًّا): The wāw is a particle of oath and genitive; الصافات is genitive by the wāw of the oath; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to an omitted verb, its implied form being "I swear" (أقسم). الصافات is the active participle of صف. It is said that they are the angels lined up in heaven glorifying, having ranks upon which they stand in rows, as worshippers line up in prayer; it is said that they are the fighters in the way of Allah; it is said they are the worshippers at prayer; and it is said that it is the birds spreading their wings, as in His saying «والطير صافات». In الصافات there is a latent pronoun that is the fāʿil (agent), and the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) is omitted, i.e. "themselves" or "their wings". صفا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) of emphasis.
(فَالزَّاجِراتِ زَجْراً): The fāʾ is a conjunction. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: what is the rule of the fāʾ when it comes as a conjunction among attributes? I say: either it indicates the succession of their meanings in existence, as in the verse:
يا لهف زيابة للحارث الصا ... بح فالغانم فالآيب
(Alas for Ziyāba, for al-Ḥārith — the one who raids at dawn, then takes spoil, then returns.)
as if it were said: the one who raided at dawn, then took booty, then returned; or it indicates their succession in degrees of excellence in some respects, as you say 'take the best, then the most perfect' and 'do the best, then the most beautiful'; or it indicates the succession of the things described in that, as in the saying 'May Allah have mercy on those who shave, then on those who shorten.' By these three principles the matter of the conjunctive fāʾ among attributes proceeds. A useful follow-up to this exposition will come in the chapter on Rhetoric."
الزاجرات is conjoined to الصافات. It is said that what is meant by it is the souls of the scholars, because they rebuke the disobedient with counsel and admonition; or the angels driving the clouds, i.e. propelling them. زجرا is likewise a verbal noun of emphasis. (فَالتَّالِياتِ ذِكْراً): It is said that He meant the souls of the scholars because they recite the verses of Allah and study His laws; and it is said that He meant the souls of the commanders of the fighters in the way of Allah, who draw up the ranks, rebuke the horses and recite the Remembrance, none of those preoccupations distracting them from it. ذكرا is a mafʿūl muṭlaq because التاليات has the meaning of "reciters"; and it is also permissible that it be a mafʿūl bihi of التاليات. The meaning of the oath by these things will come in the chapter on Benefits.
(إِنَّ إِلهَكُمْ لَواحِدٌ): The clause has no grammatical position because it is the answer to the oath. إن and its noun, the shifted lām, and واحد is its khabar.
(رَبُّ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَما بَيْنَهُما وَرَبُّ الْمَشارِقِ): رب السموات is a badal (substitute) of واحد, or a second khabar, or the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ. ما is conjoined to السموات; the adverbial is attached to an omitted ṣila of the relative noun. ورب المشارق is conjoined to رب السموات. The secret of repeating "Lord" and of not mentioning the places of setting will come in the chapter on Rhetoric.
(إِنَّا زَيَّنَّا السَّماءَ الدُّنْيا بِزِينَةٍ الْكَواكِبِ): A resumptive utterance, brought to establish the subtleties of His craft and the wonder of His creation. إن and its noun, and the clause زينا is its khabar; زينا is a past verb, نا is the fāʿil, السماء is the mafʿūl bihi, الدنيا is an adjective, meaning "the one nearest to you and which appears to your eyes", and it is worthy of reflection and consideration. بزينة is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to زينا, and الكواكب is an ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition) or a badal of زينة. There are other readings and interesting parsings which we shall present in the chapter on Benefits.
(وَحِفْظاً مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْطانٍ مارِدٍ): The wāw is a conjunction. In the accusative of حفظا there are several aspects, the most elevated of them in meaning being what al-Zamakhsharī inclined to. He said: "وحفظا is carried over on the meaning, because the meaning is: We created the stars as an adornment for the heaven and a protection from the devil, as the Exalted said: «ولقد زينا السماء الدنيا بمصابيح وجعلناها رجوما للشياطين». It is also permissible to suppose the verb which this is the reason for, as if it were said: 'and as protection from every devil We adorned it with the stars'; and it is said: 'and We protected it with a protection'." This second aspect is easier as regards the parsing. Al-Shihāb al-Ḥalabī, known as al-Samīn, said: "وحفظا is either accusative as a verbal noun by implying a verb, i.e. 'We protected it a protection'; or as a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose) with the wāw redundant, the governing agent in it being زينا; or the governing agent is implied, i.e. 'for its protection We adorned it'; or by carrying it over on the preceding meaning, i.e. 'We created the lowest heaven as an adornment and a protection'." Abū l-Baqāʾ confined himself to its being a mafʿūl muṭlaq. من كل شيطان is attached to حفظا if it is not a verbal noun of emphasis, and to an omitted element if it is made a verbal noun of emphasis; it is also permissible that it be an adjective of حفظا.
(لا يَسَّمَّعُونَ إِلَى الْمَلَإِ الْأَعْلى وَيُقْذَفُونَ مِنْ كُلِّ جانِبٍ): In the parsing of this clause there is much discussion and long debate, which we defer to the chapter on Benefits. لا is a negative particle; يسمعون is an imperfect verb, nominative, its sign of nominative being the retention of the nūn; the wāw is the fāʿil; إلى الملأ الأعلى is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to يسمعون (the secret of this transitivity will come in the chapter on Benefits); الأعلى is an adjective of الملأ. ويقذفون: the wāw is a conjunction; يقذفون is a passive imperfect verb, the wāw is the nāʾib fāʿil; من كل جانب is attached to يقذفون, i.e. from whatever direction they ascend in order to eavesdrop.
(دُحُوراً وَلَهُمْ عَذابٌ واصِبٌ): دحورا is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi, i.e. "they are pelted for the sake of driving them away"; or "as ones driven away", as a ḥāl; or a mafʿūl muṭlaq, a synonym standing in for the verbal noun, since pelting and driving away are close in meaning. The wāw is a conjunction; ولهم is a predicate put forward; عذاب is a mubtadaʾ put later; واصب is an adjective of عذاب.
(إِلَّا مَنْ خَطِفَ الْخَطْفَةَ فَأَتْبَعَهُ شِهابٌ ثاقِبٌ): إلا is a particle of restriction and exception, because the utterance is complete and negative. من is in the position of nominative as a badal of the wāw according to the first view, or in the position of accusative as the excepted according to the second; the exception may also be discontinuous (munqaṭiʿ), in which case the accusative as the excepted is required. الخطفة is a mafʿūl muṭlaq, being a verbal noun defined by the generic or the specific al-. فأتبعه: the fāʾ is a conjunction; أتبعه is a verb with a fronted direct object; شهاب is a fāʿil put later; ثاقب is an adjective of شهاب.

* Rhetoric:
Fronting and Postponing:
We established in the chapter on I'rab al-Zamakhsharī's exposition of the conjunctive fāʾ among attributes. Al-Zamakhsharī concluded his exposition by saying: "On this basis, if you make the thing described one, it indicates the ordering of the attributes in excellence; and if you make it three, it indicates the ordering of the things described in it. Making it one means that you hold that one class of what is mentioned in the aforementioned exegeses combines the three attributes, the first being the most excellent or the reverse; making it three means that you assign each attribute to a group, and the ranking is among the groups, either the first being the most excellent or the reverse." Al-Zamakhsharī's position is strong and his exposition enjoyable and useful, but he did not explain the aspect of each of the two. The gist of what may be said about it is that the Arabs have two approaches to fronting. The first:
1- Concern for the more important: they put first what is more deserving of attention and fitter to strike the ear.
2- Ascending from the lower to the higher, as in the verse:
بهاليل منهم جعفر وابن أمه ... علي ومنهم أحمد المتخير
(Noble lords, among them Jaʿfar and his mother's son ʿAlī, and among them Aḥmad the chosen.)
It is not to be said that this was permissible only because the wāw does not require order, for that at most is an excuse, whereas what we have mentioned is an explanation of the demands of badīʿ (rhetorical embellishment) and eloquence in it.
A general word on fronting and postponing:
ʿAbd al-Qāhir devoted a lengthy section in his book Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz to fronting and postponing, to which the reader may refer if he wishes. We summarise here what the scholars of ʿilm al-maʿānī said on the subject. It is known that the parts of speech cannot be pronounced all at once; rather some parts must come first and others later, and none of them is in itself more deserving to come first than another, since all words, as words, share the same degree of consideration. So there must be a motive requiring the fronting of this over that, and these motives are many, among them:
1- Arousing eagerness for the postponed element, when the postponed element signals something strange, as in the verse of Abū l-ʿAlāʾ:
والذي حارت البرية فيه ... حيوان مستحدث من جماد
(And that over which creation is bewildered: a living being newly produced from inanimate matter.)
2- Hastening joy or grief, as in: العفو عنك صدر به الأمر (pardon for you is what the order was issued with) or القصاص حكم به القاضي (retaliation is what the judge ruled).
3- The fronted element being the point of denial and wonder, as in: أبعد طول التجربة تنخدع؟ ("After such long experience are you deceived?")
4- Stating explicitly the generality of negation or the negation of generality. The first is by putting the particle of generality before the particle of negation, as in: كل ذلك لم يقع, i.e. neither this nor that occurred; the second is by putting the particle of negation before the particle of generality, as in: لم يكن كل ذلك, i.e. the whole did not occur, so it admits the occurrence of some, and admits the negation of every single one.
5- Specification, as in: ما أنا قلت, and إياك نعبد.
6- Among what ʿAbd al-Qāhir holds is the fronting of the noun in it as something virtually necessary, as with (مثل) and (غير) in the verse:
مثلك يثني المزن عن صوبه ... ويسترد الدمع عن غربه
(One like you turns the rain-cloud from its downpour and draws back the tear from its flow.)
and Abū Tammām's verse:
وغيري يأكل المعروف سحتا ... وتشجب عنده بيض الأيادي
(Another than I devours kindness as unlawful gain, and white bounties are wasted with him.)
In the first expression مثل is not meant to refer to any person other than the one to whom it is annexed; rather they mean that whoever was like him in state and attribute, it would be by analogy and by custom and convention required that he do what is mentioned or not do it. Likewise in the second expression, غير is not meant to point to a person of whom it is reported that he does so; rather he only meant to say: "I am not one of those who devour kindness as unlawful gain."

* Benefits:
1- The wāw in this construction:
The position of Sībawayh and al-Khalīl, in cases such as «والليل إذا يغشى والنهار إذا تجلى», is that the second wāw and what follows are conjunctions, whereas others than al-Khalīl and Sībawayh hold that they are particles of oath. So the occurrence of the fāʾ in «والصافات صفا فالزاجرات زجرا فالتاليات ذكرا» in the place of the wāw, the meaning being one, except for the ordering that the fāʾ adds, is clear evidence that the wāw occurring in such a context is for conjunction, not for oath.
2- The meaning of the oath:
People differed over what is sworn by. The preferred view is that what is sworn by is these things themselves, because of the apparent wording, and departing from it is contrary to the evidence. As for the prohibition on swearing by other than Allah, it is a prohibition addressed to the created being to do so. The second view is that what is sworn by is the Lord of these things, because of his ﷺ prohibition of swearing by other than Allah the Exalted, so the word "Lord" must be implied, the speech being understood as "and by the Lord of those who line up in rows..." and so on. In any case, this oath contains an exaltation of these things and a magnification of them, and more on this discussion will come.
3- On the parsing of «بزينة الكواكب»:
Al-Shihāb al-Ḥalabī, known as al-Samīn, said: "His saying «بزينة الكواكب»: Abū Bakr read it with tanwīn on زينة and the accusative of الكواكب. It has two aspects: one, that الزينة is a verbal noun whose agent is omitted, the implied form being 'in that Allah adorned the stars, in their being luminous and beautiful in themselves'; the second, that الزينة is a noun for that by which something is adorned, like الليقة for what the inkwell is made to adhere with, so الكواكب on this basis is accusative by implying 'I mean', or is a badal of سماء الدنيا (a badal of inclusion, i.e. 'its stars'), or of the position of بزينة. Ḥamza and Ḥafṣ read likewise except that they put الكواكب in the genitive, meaning by زينة that by which one adorns, with الكواكب a badal or explication of الزينة. The others read it with annexation of زينة to الكواكب, which admits three aspects: first, that it is an annexation of the more general to the more specific, so it is explicative, as in 'a garment of silk'; second, that it is a verbal noun annexed to its agent, i.e. 'in that the stars adorned the heaven with their light'; third, that it is annexed to its object, i.e. 'in that Allah adorned it by making it bright and luminous in itself'."
4- The parsing of the clause لا يسمعون:
The parsers, exegetes and grammarians went at length over the parsing of this clause, and we cite here selections from the sayings of the well-known among them, beginning with al-Zamakhsharī:
"If you ask: how does «لا يسمعون» connect with what precedes it? I say: it cannot be other than connected with what precedes either as an adjective of «كل شيطان» or as a resumption. The adjective is not sound, because protection from devils who neither hear nor eavesdrop has no meaning; and likewise the resumption, because if a questioner asked 'Why is protection made from the devils?' and it were answered that they do not hear, it would not hold. So it remains that it is a detached, newly begun utterance, relating the state of those who steal a hearing, that they are unable to hear the speech of the angels or to listen in, being pelted with meteors and driven away from that — except that whoever is given respite until he snatches a snatch and steals a theft, then destruction overtakes him by the following of the piercing flame." Al-Zamakhsharī went on in his exposition, saying: "If you ask: is the claim valid of one who alleges that the origin was «لئلا يسمعوا», the lām being dropped as it is dropped in your saying 'I came to you that you might honour me', leaving «أن لا يسمعوا», then أن was dropped and its operation disregarded, as in the verse of Ṭarafa:
ألا أيها ذا الزاجري أحضر الوغى ... وأن اشهد اللذات هل أنت مخلدي
(O you who forbid me to attend the battle and to witness pleasures — are you going to make me immortal?)
I say: each of these two omissions is not rejected on its own; but their combination is one of the abominations; and the Qur'an should be preserved from such artifice."
Ibn al-Munayyir, author of al-Intiṣāf, followed him up and said: "Both aspects are sound. The answer to his difficulty raised against the first aspect is that the devil's not hearing is caused by the protection from him, so the devil's state as one protected from is his state as one who does not hear, and one state is concomitant with the other; so there is no obstacle to the protection from him and his being described as not hearing combining in one state, not on the basis that the not-hearing is established before the protection, but with it and concurrent with it. A parallel to this verse is the saying of the Exalted: «وسخر لكم الليل والنهار والشمس والقمر والنجوم مسخرات بأمره». His saying «مسخرات» is a ḥāl from what precedes it, the agent in it being the verb سخر, and its meaning is sound, because His subjecting them entails their being subjected; the state in which they were subjected is the state in which they were subjected-ones, not in the sense of His subjecting them while they were already subjected before. What al-Zamakhsharī indicated in this verse is close to this explanation, except that he mentioned along with it another interpretation, as though finding this aspect problematic: he made «مسخرات» the plural of مسخر, a verbal noun like ممزّق, and made the meaning 'He subjected to you the night, the day, the sun and the moon, in kinds of subjection'. What we have mentioned suffices. Of this type is «ثم أرسلنا رسلنا»: they were not messengers except by the sending, and these were not non-hearers except by the protection. As for the answer to his second difficulty, a double omission occurs in such as the saying of the Exalted «يبين الله لكم أن تضلوا», the origin being «لئلا تضلوا», in which the lām and lā were both dropped from their places."
Al-Shihāb al-Ḥalabī, known as al-Samīn, said: "This clause is cut off from what precedes in the parsing. It cannot be an adjective of «شيطان» in meaning, since the estimate would become 'from every rebellious devil not hearing or listening', which is invalid. Nor can it be an answer to a questioner's 'Why is protection made from the devil?', since that would spoil the meaning. Some said: the original was «لئلا يسمعوا», the lām and أن were dropped and the verb became nominative, but this is artifice. Abū l-Baqāʾ erred in allowing it to be an adjective, a ḥāl, or resumptive: the first two are plainly invalid, and the third, if he meant the explanatory resumption, is also invalid, while if he meant detachment as I have presented, it is sound."
As for Abū l-Baqāʾ's statement which al-Samīn disparaged, it is: "His saying the Exalted «لا يسمعون» is in the plural on the sense of «كل»; the position of the clause is genitive as an adjective, or accusative as a ḥāl, or resumptive; and he made it transitive with إلى by carrying it over to the sense of 'listening' (يصغون)."
As for Ibn Hishām, he devoted a special note to this clause in al-Mughnī, saying: "Among resumptions are some that may be hidden, and they have many examples. One is «لا يسمعون» from the saying of the Exalted «وحفظا من كل شيطان مارد لا يسمعون إلى الملأ الأعلى». What first comes to mind is that it is an adjective of «كل شيطان» or a ḥāl from it, but both are invalid, since there is no meaning in protection from a devil who does not hear. It is rather a grammatical resumption, and it cannot be an explanatory resumption, again because the meaning would be spoiled. It has been said that the original may be «لئلا يسمعوا», then the lām was dropped as in 'I came to you that you honour me', then أن was dropped and the verb became nominative as in the verse:
ألا أيها ذا الزاجري احضر الوغى ... ......
where 'aḥḍuru' was put in the nominative. Al-Zamakhsharī considered the combination of the two omissions weak. If you say: make it an anticipated ḥāl, i.e. 'and as protection from every rebellious devil, with his non-hearing anticipated after the protection', I say: the one who anticipates the existence of the meaning of the ḥāl is its owner, as with the one passed by in your saying 'I passed by a man with a falcon hunting with it tomorrow', that is, one who is bound in the state of passing to hunt tomorrow; whereas the devils neither anticipate not hearing nor wish it."
An important remark:
Resumption is of two kinds: explanatory (bayānī) and grammatical (naḥwī). The explanatory is what is an answer to an implied question, as in the saying of the Exalted: «هل أتاك حديث ضيف إبراهيم المكرمين إذ دخلوا عليه فقالوا: سلاما قال سلام قوم منكرون». The second clause of speech is the answer to an implied question, whose estimate is "And what did he say to them?" and for this reason it was separated from the first and not conjoined to it. The grammarians, however, said: it is that which is cut off from what precedes it, whether or not it is an answer to a question, so resumption in their view is more general.
Al-Damāmīnī then rebutted Ibn Hishām, saying: "If it is for grammatical resumption, then he has reported of the devils, from whom precaution is taken, that they do not hear, and then the difficulty returns: how can precaution be taken against a devil who in reality did not hear, since the one precaution is taken against is one who hears? If you say: what is meant is that they do not hear after the protection, we say: estimate that in the adjective and the meaning is free of obstruction; so why did you estimate it in the grammatical resumption and not in the adjective, when the meaning is in any case clear? This is arbitrariness." Al-Shumunnī answered that it is a report on the state of the devils, not describing their being protected from; against which it is said that it is not valid to report of them non-hearing apart from the protection, because they are protected in reality, and non-hearing derives only from protection, otherwise protection would have no meaning.
What led us to cite these views is the mental exercise in them; and perhaps Ibn al-Munayyir has spared us the trouble of refuting them, so refer to him and ponder him, for he has hit the mark.
A subtle distinction:
Al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: what is the difference between سمعت فلانا يتحدث and سمعت إليه يتحدث, and between سمعت حديثه and إلى حديثه? I say: what is made transitive by itself indicates perception, and what is made transitive by إلى indicates listening attentively along with perception."

dervis-irab:11-19.t:
* Vocabulary:
(فَاسْتَفْتِهِمْ): i.e. فاستخبرهم, "so ask them for information". One says استفتى استفتاء العالم في مسألة: he asked him to give a legal ruling on it. الفتوى, الفتوى and الفتيا are nouns from أفتى العالم, when the scholar made the ruling clear; the plural is الفتاوي and الفتاوى.
(لازِبٍ): binding, adhering. One says لزب يلزب لزوبا, from the pattern of دخل: it became intense and firm; and لزب به: it stuck to it. And لزب يلزب لزبا, from the pattern of تعب; and لزب يلزب لزبا and لزوبا, from the pattern of كرم, said of clay: it stuck and hardened. لزب الشيء: parts of it entered into other parts. اللازم is an active participle, "the firm one". One says صار الأمر ضربة لازب, i.e. the matter became binding and firm; and طين لازب is clay that sticks to the hand because of its toughness. In al-Mukhtār: "You say: صار الشيء لازبا, i.e. firm, and it is more eloquent than لازما." Al-Nābigha said:
ولا تحسبون الخير لا شر بعده ... ولا تحسبون الشر ضربة لازب
(Do not suppose that good has no evil after it, and do not suppose that evil is a binding blow.)
(داخِرُونَ): abject. One says دخر يدخر, from the pattern of فتح, and دخر يدخر, from the pattern of تعب, dakhran and dukhūran, i.e. he was humbled and became small.

* I'rab:
(فَاسْتَفْتِهِمْ أَهُمْ أَشَدُّ خَلْقاً أَمْ مَنْ خَلَقْنا): The fāʾ is the "eloquent fāʾ" (al-fāʾ al-faṣīḥa), i.e. "if you wish to rebuke them and answer them concerning the establishment of the Return, then ask them for a ruling", because the difference is clear and the gap wide between the Return, which is the original parts, as will come. «[Translator's note: the sentence reads as if incomplete in the source.]» You may also make it the conjunctive fāʾ of sequence, i.e. "ask them for a ruling after the enumeration of these things mentioned above". فاستفتهم is an imperative verb, indeclinable by the omission of the weak letter; the fāʿil is a latent pronoun, necessarily so, its implied form being "you"; the hāʾ is the mafʿūl bihi. The hamza is for interrogation; هم is the mubtadaʾ, أشد the khabar, خلقا a tamyīz (specification). أم is a conjunction, here the connected (muttaṣila) kind; مَن is conjoined to هم, and the clause خلقنا is the ṣila of the relative noun. (إِنَّا خَلَقْناهُمْ مِنْ طِينٍ لازِبٍ): إن and its noun, and the clause خلقناهم is the khabar; خلقناهم is a verb, agent and object; من طين is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to خلقناهم; لازب is an adjective of طين. And this suffices you as proof of their weakness, namely their condition and the insignificance of their standing, and that whoever is of such a rank cannot be arrogant and haughty. (بَلْ عَجِبْتَ وَيَسْخَرُونَ): بل is a particle of rejection and conjunction, and the conjoined-to is implied, indicated by the interrogative, i.e. "they do not admit it". عجبت is a verb and agent, the address being to the Prophet; the thing it is attached to is omitted, i.e. "at the power of Allah over these mighty creatures". In one reading, with ḍamma on the tāʾ, the attribution of wonder to Allah the Exalted is impossible, because wonder is an amazement that overcomes a human being when he deems something great, and that is impossible for Allah the Exalted; but the speech proceeds by way of imagining wonder and supposing it, by way of mushākala (correspondence), examples of which have preceded.
The wāw is circumstantial, and the clause يسخرون is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "and they are mocking", the clause being accusative as a ḥāl.
(وَإِذا ذُكِّرُوا لا يَذْكُرُونَ): The wāw is a conjunction; إذا is a future adverb containing the sense of condition; the clause ذكروا is in the position of genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it; ذكروا is passive with shadda, the wāw being the nāʾib fāʿil; لا is negative; and the clause لا يذكرون has no grammatical position because it is the apodosis of a non-jussive condition, i.e. "their habit is not to take admonition from anything, however worthy of consideration." (وَإِذا رَأَوْا آيَةً يَسْتَسْخِرُونَ): Conjoined to what precedes. By "sign" is meant the miracle that calls to submission, but miracles have no effect on these people. The meaning of الاستسخار is that they call one another to mockery, or that the addition of the sīn and tāʾ is merely for intensification of mocking. (وَقالُوا إِنْ هذا إِلَّا سِحْرٌ مُبِينٌ): The wāw is a conjunction; قالوا is a verb and agent; إن is negative; هذا is the mubtadaʾ; إلا is a particle of restriction; سحر is the khabar of هذا; مبين is an adjective, i.e. "plain to the eye"; and the clause is the content of the saying. (أَإِذا مِتْنا وَكُنَّا تُراباً وَعِظاماً أَإِنَّا لَمَبْعُوثُونَ): The clause is the content of an omitted saying also, i.e. "and they said, denying the resurrection". The hamza is for denying interrogation; إذا is a future adverb containing the sense of condition; the clause متنا is in the position of genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it; كنا is an incomplete past verb, نا its noun, ترابا its khabar, عظاما conjoined to ترابا; the hamza is also for denying interrogation; ان and its noun, the shifted lām, and مبعوثون is its khabar.
(أَوَآباؤُنَا الْأَوَّلُونَ): The hamza is for interrogation; the wāw is a conjunction; آباؤنا is conjoined to the position of إن and its noun, or to the pronoun in مبعوثون. The conjunction is permissible although what follows the interrogative hamza is not governed by what precedes it, because the second hamza is emphasis of the first and is in intention fronted, so what precedes it can govern what follows it. You may also parse آباؤنا as a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted, the estimate being "or will our fathers be raised too?". It was also read أو with sukūn on the wāw, in which case it is a conjunction and there is no interrogative hamza. What follows is al-Samīn's exposition on this verse: "His saying «أو آباؤنا»: Ibn ʿĀmir read it with sukūn on the wāw, as the conjunctive «أو» that indicates doubt, and the others with fatḥa, as an interrogative hamza that entered upon the conjunctive wāw. This difference also occurs in al-Wāqiʿa, and the like has preceded in al-Aʿrāf in His saying «أو أمن أهل القرى». Whoever vocalised the wāw with fatḥa allowed two aspects in «آبائنا»: one, that it is conjoined to the position of إن and its noun; the other, that it is conjoined to the latent pronoun in «لمبعوثون», being sufficed by the separation made by the interrogative hamza. Whoever put sukūn on it, the first is required and not the second, according to the majority, for lack of a separator." (قُلْ: نَعَمْ وَأَنْتُمْ داخِرُونَ): قل is an imperative verb, its agent a latent pronoun whose implied form is "you"; نعم is a particle of response; the wāw is circumstantial; أنتم is the mubtadaʾ and داخرون the khabar; the clause is accusative as a ḥāl, and its governing agent is نعم with regard to its meaning, i.e. "Yes, you will be raised while you are abject."
(فَإِنَّما هِيَ زَجْرَةٌ واحِدَةٌ فَإِذا هُمْ يَنْظُرُونَ): The fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ, because it occurs in the answer to an implied condition whose estimate is "if that is so, then it is only...". إنما: ما is the preventive (kāffa) and إن is the prevented; هي is the mubtadaʾ, زجرة the khabar, واحدة an adjective. هي is an ambiguous pronoun, because it does not refer back to anything, and only its khabar clarifies it. They permitted that هي refer back to the "raising" indicated by the context; since their raising results from the shout, it was made figuratively the same as it. الزجرة is the frightening cry. The poet said:
زجر أبي عروة السباع إذا ... أشفقن أن يختلطن بالغنم
(Like Abū ʿUrwa's rebuking of the beasts of prey when they feared they would mingle with the sheep.)
He means his shouting with it. The fāʾ is a conjunction; إذا is a sudden "idhā"; هم is the mubtadaʾ and the clause ينظرون the khabar, its object being omitted, i.e. "they look at what will be done to them", or it has the sense of "they wait".

dervis-irab:157-164.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْجِنَّةِ) : With kasra on the jīm: the angels. They were so named because of their concealment from sight (ijtinān). In al-Asās: "«جنة»: he screened him, so he became concealed, and «استجن بجنة» means he took cover with a shield; «اجتن الولد في البطن» means the child was hidden in the womb, and the pregnant woman concealed it («أجنّته»); and how excellent is a shield (mijann) like Ibn Abī Rabīʿa!"

* I'rab:
(فَأْتُوا بِكِتابِكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ)
The fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa (the eloquent fāʾ); «أْتُوا» is an imperative verb indeclinable by deletion of the nūn, and the wāw is the agent; «بِكِتابِكُمْ» is attached to it; «إِنْ» is conditional; «كُنْتُمْ» is a defective past verb, the tāʾ is its noun and «صادِقِينَ» its predicate; the apodosis is omitted, indicated by what precedes. (وَجَعَلُوا بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ الْجِنَّةِ نَسَباً) The wāw is resumptive, and the discourse is resumptive, introduced to cast blame upon them and to charge their minds with feebleness, in that those whom they ascribed to Allah the Exalted know their own grievous fates. «جَعَلُوا» is a verb and an agent; the adverbial is attached to an omitted element which is the second direct object of «جَعَلُوا»; «وَبَيْنَ الْجِنَّةِ» is conjoined, and «نَسَباً» is the first direct object of «جَعَلُوا». It is therefore a report that must be broadcast and spread, so as to be a witness to the reality of their madness. (وَلَقَدْ عَلِمَتِ الْجِنَّةُ إِنَّهُمْ لَمُحْضَرُونَ) The wāw is circumstantial; the lām is the answer to an omitted oath; «قَدْ» is a particle of certainty; «عَلِمَتِ الْجِنَّةُ» is a verb and an agent; inna and its noun, the shifted lām, and «مُحْضَرُونَ» is its predicate; inna and what follows it stand in the place of the two objects of «عَلِمَتِ». Its hamza has the kasra only because the lām has entered its predicate. The pronoun in «إِنَّهُمْ لَمُحْضَرُونَ» refers to the disbelievers. The meaning is that they say what they say about the angels, while the angels know that they are lying in that nonsensical statement.
(سُبْحانَ اللَّهِ عَمَّا يَصِفُونَ) «سُبْحانَ اللَّهِ» is a mafʿūl muṭlaq of an omitted verb; «عَمَّا» is attached to «سُبْحانَ»; the clause «يَصِفُونَ» is a ṣila, its returning pronoun omitted; the clause is parenthetical, introduced to relate the angels' declaration of Allah's transcendence, glory be to Him, above what the polytheists ascribe to Him. (إِلَّا عِبادَ اللَّهِ الْمُخْلَصِينَ) «إِلَّا» is a particle of exception; «عِبادَ اللَّهِ الْمُخْلَصِينَ» is a discontinuous exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ) from «الْمُحْضَرُونَ», as though they were not among them. The thing excepted from is either the agent of «جَعَلُوا», or the agent of «يَصِفُونَ», or the pronoun of «مُحْضَرُونَ»; that is, "but the sincere servants of Allah are saved". It is also permissible that the exception be continuous (muttaṣil); Abū al-Baqāʾ preferred it, and it is not far-fetched. (فَإِنَّكُمْ وَما تَعْبُدُونَ، ما أَنْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ بِفاتِنِينَ) The fāʾ is causal; inna and its noun; the wāw is the wāw of accompaniment; «ما» is a relative noun, a mafʿūl maʿahu, and it stands in the place of the predicate of inna, that is, "you and your gods are companions, and you continue to worship them", on the pattern of your saying «كل رجل وصنيعته» ("every man and his craft"), meaning "the two are paired"; the details of this rule will come in the section on Benefits. «ما» is the Ḥijāzī negative; «أَنْتُمْ» is its noun; «عَلَيْهِ» is attached to «فاتِنِينَ»; the bāʾ is a redundant preposition, and «فاتِنِينَ» is the predicate of «ما». It is also permissible that «ما» be conjoined to the noun of inna and the clause «ما أَنْتُمْ» be the khabar of inna; the meaning on this view is "you and what you worship, you do not lead astray, nor does it", and the addressee was given precedence. It is said «فتن فلان على فلان امرأته» ("so-and-so corrupted his wife against so-and-so"), meaning he ruined her for him. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Bayḍāwī preferred this view.
(إِلَّا مَنْ هُوَ صالِ الْجَحِيمِ) «إِلَّا» is a particle of restriction, and «مَنْ» is the object of «فاتِنِينَ»; the exception is exceptive of the omitted-excepted-from kind (mufarragh). It is also permissible to posit an object of «فاتِنِينَ», namely "anyone", so that «إِلَّا» is a particle of exception and «مَنْ» is excepted from the omitted object. «هُوَ» is a mubtadaʾ and «صالِ» a khabar, in the nominative with an implied ḍamma on the omitted yāʾ because of the meeting of two quiescent letters; «الْجَحِيمِ» is a muḍāf ilayhi.
