The well-known gender is feminine, and it was said to be masculine; and its pattern, on the ... fuʿlā [Translator's note: the source reads «على الباعث فعلى»; the wording appears corrupt], so it is a diptote whether it is used as a name or not, unless one affirms fiʿlal, in which case it is declined when indefinite. And Allah knows best.

dervis-irab:123-132.t:
* Vocabulary:
(بَعْلًا): Baʿl is the name of an idol of theirs made of gold, and the town too was named after it, annexed to Bakk, which was originally the name of the town; then, when this idol called Baʿl was worshipped in it, it was named Baʿlabakk. In Tāj al-ʿArūs: "Al-Azharī said: they are two names made one name for a city in Syria, and the relative adjective for it is baʿlī or bakkī, as mentioned under ʿAbd Shams." The wording of al-Zamakhsharī: "'Do you call upon Baʿl' is the name of an idol they had, like Manāt and Hubal. It was said that it was of gold, twenty cubits tall, with four faces; they were tempted by it and glorified it until they assigned it four hundred attendants and made them its prophets. Satan would enter Baʿl's interior and speak a law of error, which the attendants would memorise and teach to the people, and they were the people of Baʿlabakk in the land of Syria, and their city was named Baʿlabakk after it. It was also said that al-baʿl is the lord in the language of Yemen; one says: 'man baʿl hādhihi al-dār?', i.e. who is its lord?" More of this story will come in the section on benefits.
(تَدْعُونَ): you call.
(تَذَرُونَ): you leave. We have heard from one who has standing in Arabic that the two words dhar and daʿ are both commands in the sense of leaving, except that daʿ is a command to the one addressed to leave a thing before knowing it, while dhar is a command to leave it after he has known it. It is narrated that one of the imams asked Imam al-Rāzī about His saying, the Exalted: «أتدعون بعلا وتذرون أحسن الخالقين», why He did not say "wa-tadʿūna aḥsana l-khāliqīn", which would be closer to eloquence because of the paronomasia between them. The Imam said: because they took the idols as gods and left Allah after they had known that Allah is their Lord and the Lord of their earlier fathers, out of arrogance; for that reason it was said to them "and you leave" and not "and you call". The Arabs, however, let the past tense of daʿ and dhar and their verbal nouns fall into disuse, but it is narrated in the hadith: "Peoples will surely cease from their wadʿihim of the Friday prayers", i.e. from their leaving the Friday prayers. And he said in al-Qāmūs:
waddaʿahu, i.e. "leave it": its origin is waddaʿa, like waḍaʿa, and its past tense has been allowed to die; one says in its past tense only tarakahu (he left it). In poetry waddaʿahu occurs, and mawdūʿ; and it was read as an irregular reading:
«ما ودّعك ربك», which is the reading of the Prophet ﷺ. And al-Jawharī said:
one does not say wādiʿ, but its occurrence in poetry and in the reading contradicts that, unless their saying "its past tense has been allowed to die" is taken to mean rarity of use, so that it is irregular in usage but sound by analogy.
(إِلْ ياسِينَ): Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It has been read ʿalā l-Yāsīn, Idrīsīn and Idārisīn and Idrīsīn, as dialectal variants of Ilyās and Idrīs, and perhaps the added yāʾ and nūn have a meaning in Syriac." It was also said that what is meant by Yāsīn is this same Ilyās that preceded; on this it is singular and genitive with a fatḥa because it is a diptote, by reason of being a proper name and non-Arabic. It was also said to be him and those who believed with him, so they were combined with him by giving preponderance, as they say al-Muhallabūn for al-Muhallab; on this it is genitive with the yāʾ because it is a sound masculine plural.

* I'rab:
(وَإِنَّ إِلْياسَ لَمِنَ الْمُرْسَلِينَ) A conjunction or a resumptive passage for mentioning the fourth story. inna and its noun; Ilyās is a non-Arabic proper name whose biography will come in the section on benefits; the shifted lām; and المرسلين is the khabar.
(إِذْ قالَ لِقَوْمِهِ أَلا تَتَّقُونَ) إذ is an adverb of past time attached to an omitted verb, its implied form being "remember"; some preferred attaching it to المرسلين. The clause قال is in the position of genitive by annexation of the adverb to it; لقومه is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to قال; the hamza is for interrogation and لا is negative; تتقون is an imperfect verb in the nominative with an agent; and the clause is the content of the saying.
(أَتَدْعُونَ بَعْلًا وَتَذَرُونَ أَحْسَنَ الْخالِقِينَ) The hamza is for denial; تدعون is an imperfect verb in the nominative by the permanence of the nūn and the wāw is the agent; بعلا is the direct object; the wāw is a conjunction; تذرون is conjoined to تدعون, and it is permissible that it be circumstantial, with the clause in the position of accusative as a ḥāl; and أحسن الخالقين is the direct object.
(اللَّهَ رَبَّكُمْ وَرَبَّ آبائِكُمُ الْأَوَّلِينَ) The word of majesty is a badal from أحسن الخالقين, so it is accusative; ربكم is a badal from الله; and رب آبائكم الأولين is conjoined; so the three words are accusative. It has also been read with nominative, as khabars of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e. "He", or الله as mubtadaʾ with ربكم as its khabar and رب آبائكم الأولين conjoined to ربكم.
(فَكَذَّبُوهُ فَإِنَّهُمْ لَمُحْضَرُونَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; كذبوه is a verb, agent and direct object; the fāʾ in فإنهم is the eloquent fāʾ; inna and its noun; the shifted lām; and محضرون is the khabar of inna.
(إِلَّا عِبادَ اللَّهِ الْمُخْلَصِينَ) إلا is a particle of exception; عباد الله is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil) from the agent of فكذبوه; and المخلصين is an adjective of عباد الله.
(وَتَرَكْنا عَلَيْهِ فِي الْآخِرِينَ) Its parsing has been given recently, so renew your acquaintance with it.
(سَلامٌ عَلى إِلْ ياسِينَ) Its parsing has preceded.
(إِنَّا كَذلِكَ نَجْزِي الْمُحْسِنِينَ إِنَّهُ مِنْ عِبادِنَا الْمُؤْمِنِينَ) Its parsing has also preceded.

* Benefits:
In the story of the Prophet Ilyās there is charm, delight and artistic depiction so as to be a means of emotional influence; it addresses the religious sense of emotion in the artistic language of beauty, because the story in the Qur'an is not an independent artistic work in its subject and its manner of delivery, presentation and narration of events. Before we begin summarising the story as the biographies relate it, we begin with a glimpse of the Prophet Ilyās. The exegetes mentioned that he is a prophet among the prophets of the Children of Israel. Muhammad ibn Isḥāq said: "He is Ilyās ibn Yāsīn ibn Finḥāṣ ibn al-ʿAyzār ibn Hārūn ibn ʿImrān, and Allah knows best." In al-Munjid fī l-Ādāb wa-l-ʿUlūm it is stated that he is Elijah the prophet, one of the prophets of the Children of Israel, who fought the pagan worship that Jezebel, wife of Ahab, introduced into Israel. He was exiled to Zarephath, where he restored to life the son of a widow woman; and by Allah's permission rain fell on the earth after being withheld from it for three years, near Mount Carmel; he humiliated the priests of Baal and Ashtaroth and commanded their killing, so Jezebel pursued him with a downpour of her anger and he fled to the Sinai desert. Then he returned and prophesied to Ahab Allah's vengeance upon him because he had murdered Naboth and taken his vineyard. He was raised to heaven in a chariot of fire, and left prophethood to his disciple Elisha as successor.
What follows is a summary of what Muhammad ibn Isḥāq and the scholars of biography and reports mentioned: When Allah took the Prophet Ezekiel, grave events grew among the Children of Israel, corruption appeared among them and they set up idols, so Allah sent Ilyās to them as a prophet. Joshua, when he conquered Syria, had divided it among the tribes of Israel, and one tribe of them received in its share Baʿlabakk and its surroundings. Over them at that time was a king called Araḥb, who had led his people astray; he had an idol of gold called Baʿl. The king became angry with Ilyās and intended to torture and kill him. When Ilyās sensed the evil, he went out fleeing and took refuge in the lofty mountains and the high caves, and remained seven years wandering, spreading the earth as his bed and taking stones for a pillow, eating the plants of the earth and the fruits of trees. They had set spies on him. When the matter grew long for him and his patience was strained, he called on his Lord, and it was said: "Look on such-and-such a day and go out to such-and-such a place, and whatever comes to you, mount it." So Ilyās went out with al-Yasaʿ (Elisha), until, when he was at the place he was commanded to go to, a horse of fire approached; he leapt onto it and the horse set off with him. Al-Yasaʿ called out: "O Ilyās, what do you command me?" Ilyās threw his cloak down to him from the air, and that was the sign of his succession; and so on to the end of that wondrous story, which depicts striving for the sake of belief and steadfastness upon principle.
